site.name: Yoga Mom Talk
site.tagline: A place for moms to connect, with real help when you need it.

sections.summary: Autism, ADHD, delays and disabilities: free evaluations, school help, other parents and respite.

attribution: Disability and military-family listings are adapted from the family guide in the Veteran Resident Resource Guide, created by Travis Vought and shared by Veteran Home Guardians (CC BY 4.0).

resources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline
resources.what: Free, private support any hour of the day. An advocate can help you think through safety, shelter and next steps, whether or not you are ready to leave.
resources.how: Call, text or chat. You do not have to give your name.

resources.name: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
resources.what: Free support for anyone in emotional distress or crisis, any hour. You do not have to be thinking about suicide to call.
resources.how: Call or text 988.

resources.name: Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline
resources.what: Crisis counselors answer any hour. Call if you are worried about a child, or if you are afraid you might hurt yours.
resources.how: Call and say what is going on.

resources.name: Find your state's domestic violence coalition
resources.org: National Network to End Domestic Violence (NNEDV)
resources.what: Every state and territory has a coalition that knows the local shelters and programs. They can point you to a safe place near you.
resources.how: Open the list, choose your state, and call the coalition or the hotline it lists. Shelter addresses are kept private for safety, so this site never lists them.

resources.name: Dial 211 for local help
resources.what: A free line that connects you to local help with housing, food, utilities, child care and more.
resources.how: Dial 211, or search by ZIP code at 211.org. Say what you need and your county.

resources.name: Find a shelter near you
resources.org: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)
resources.what: A free search tool for people who need a place to stay. Type your city or ZIP code to see nearby shelters and their phone numbers. It also finds free meals, clothing and health clinics.
resources.how: Open the tool, enter where you are, and call a shelter before you go to ask about space. HUD lists these places but does not run them.

resources.name: YWCA: shelter, housing and support for women
resources.what: YWCA has 194 local associations across the country. Many run domestic violence shelters and hotlines, housing for women and families, child care and job training. What each one offers depends on where you live.
resources.how: Find your local YWCA and call to ask what it offers near you.

resources.name: Family Promise: for families with children who have lost housing
resources.what: Nearly 200 local groups in more than 40 states help families with children keep their housing, find shelter and move into a new home. Keeping the family together is a priority.
resources.how: Use the search to find the group nearest you and call its office. If there is none near you, dial 211.

resources.name: The Salvation Army: shelter and help with rent
resources.what: Emergency shelters, short-term housing and, in many places, one-time help with rent or a utility bill. Programs differ from place to place.
resources.how: Use the location search to find the center nearest you, then call to ask what help is open right now.

resources.name: Talk to a housing counselor
resources.org: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)
resources.what: Housing counseling agencies approved by HUD give free or low-cost advice on renting, eviction and foreclosure, and on what to do if you are about to lose your home.
resources.how: Call HUD's automated line to get counseling agencies near you, or search online.

resources.name: SNAP: help buying groceries
resources.org: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food and Nutrition Administration
resources.what: SNAP helps households with low income buy food. Each state runs its own program, so the website, phone number and rules depend on where you live.
resources.how: Open the state directory and choose your state. It links to your state's SNAP page and how to apply.

resources.name: WIC: food for pregnancy, babies and kids under 5
resources.org: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food and Nutrition Administration
resources.what: WIC gives healthy foods, nutrition advice, breastfeeding support and referrals at no cost. It is for women who are pregnant, recently pregnant or breastfeeding, and for babies and children under 5.
resources.how: Choose your state on the apply page, then call or apply online with a WIC agency near you. Bring ID for each person, proof of address, and proof you get SNAP, Medicaid or TANF, or proof of income.

resources.name: Help with heating and cooling bills (LIHEAP)
resources.org: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
resources.what: LIHEAP can help pay a share of your energy bills for households with low income. Rules and how to apply differ by state. Applying never costs a fee.
resources.how: Call the National Energy Assistance Referral line, weekdays 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. Eastern, or visit EnergyHelp.us. Give your city, county and state.

resources.name: Find a food bank near you
resources.what: Food banks and their partner pantries give out groceries and meals for free. Your local food bank can also tell you about SNAP and WIC.
resources.how: Enter your ZIP code. Then contact the food bank for pantry locations and hours, since they change.

resources.name: Low-cost prenatal care at a community health center
resources.org: HRSA health centers, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
resources.what: Health centers funded by HRSA charge on a sliding fee scale, so you can get care even if you are uninsured or cannot pay. Free or reduced-cost prenatal care may also be available through your area health department.
resources.how: Search by ZIP code on the HRSA site, call the center, and ask whether it provides prenatal care and what the sliding fee would be. Or call 1-800-311-BABY to find your area health department.

resources.name: Health coverage for your child: Medicaid and CHIP
resources.org: Insure Kids Now, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
resources.what: Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) cover many children in families with low or moderate income. Each state sets its own rules.
resources.how: Open the coverage page, choose your state, and follow the steps to apply. Questions can go to the national line.

resources.name: Breastfeeding questions: free helpline
resources.org: Office on Women's Health, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
resources.what: Breastfeeding peer counselors answer questions, help with common problems and point you to other help, in English or Spanish. It is an information line and does not give medical advice.
resources.how: Call Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern; it is closed on federal holidays. WIC also offers breastfeeding support.

resources.name: La Leche League: breastfeeding support from other parents
resources.what: Meetings and one-to-one help led by trained volunteer Leaders, who have breastfed their own babies. A map shows groups and Leaders near you and online.
resources.how: Open the map, allow your location or search your area, and contact a Leader. Ask whether there is any cost.

resources.name: Free diapers from a diaper bank
resources.org: National Diaper Bank Network member banks
resources.what: Diaper banks collect and give out free diapers to families who struggle to afford them. The national directory lists member banks by state and city.
resources.how: Open the directory, find your state, and contact the bank nearest you to ask how to sign up. Rules differ by bank. If none is close, dial 211 and ask about diaper help.

resources.name: Safe sleep for your baby
resources.org: Safe to Sleep campaign, National Institutes of Health
resources.what: Put your baby to sleep on their back, on a firm, flat surface made for babies, with nothing soft in the sleep space. This lowers the risk of sleep-related death.
resources.how: Read the short guides, in English and Spanish, before the first night home.

resources.name: Child care help, licensing and child support: your state's page
resources.org: ChildCare.gov, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
resources.what: One page per state gathers links for finding licensed child care, help paying for it, child support, health coverage and more.
resources.how: Open the state list and choose your state. Use the link to your state's child care search to find providers near you.

resources.name: Head Start and Early Head Start: free early learning
resources.org: Office of Head Start, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
resources.what: Free learning and development for children from birth to age 5 in eligible families. Early Head Start serves babies and toddlers, and some programs also serve pregnant women. All programs welcome children with disabilities.
resources.how: Use the center locator, then call the program listed and ask how to enroll. If there is no space, ask to be added to the waiting list.

resources.name: Free legal help: custody, divorce, housing and benefits
resources.what: Legal aid offices help people with low income with family law, eviction, benefits and more, at no cost. Rules about who qualifies depend on the office.
resources.how: Use the Legal Services Corporation finder to reach the program for your area. LawHelp.org also has state-by-state guides, forms and local contacts.

resources.name: Find a kinship navigator in your state
resources.org: Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
resources.what: Kinship navigators help relatives raising children find benefits, legal help and services, then follow up with you. This federal list names the known programs in each state and for tribes, and who each one serves.
resources.how: Open the list, find your state, and call or write to the program. Tell them who is living with you and what you need first.

resources.name: GrandFacts: your state's fact sheet for relatives raising children
resources.what: A short fact sheet for each state on the programs, public benefits, school help and legal options for grandparents and other relatives raising children. There are sheets for D.C., Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, and one in Spanish.
resources.how: Open your state's sheet and keep it handy. It lists the programs and benefits to ask about and the legal options in your state, such as custody and guardianship.

resources.name: Cash help for the child (TANF "child-only")
resources.org: Your state's TANF program, overseen by the U.S. Administration for Children and Families
resources.what: TANF, the cash assistance program for families, can help children who live with relatives. A grant for the child alone is often called a child-only case.
resources.how: Apply where your state takes cash assistance applications and ask about a child-only grant for the children in your care. Your state's GrandFacts sheet lists its public benefits.

resources.name: Becoming a licensed kinship foster parent
resources.org: Children's Bureau, U.S. Administration for Children and Families
resources.what: If children services placed the child with you, ask whether you can become a licensed foster parent. Since 2023, states may use licensing standards made for relatives, and licensed relative homes get the same foster care payments as other licensed foster homes.
resources.how: Ask the caseworker what licensing would mean for your family, what the payments are, and how it compares with legal custody or guardianship. Free legal aid can help you decide.

resources.name: Support for grandparents and relatives 55 and older
resources.what: Relatives 55 and older raising a child under 18 can get support groups, counseling, caregiver training and a break (respite) through their local Area Agency on Aging. It is the National Family Caregiver Support Program, for relatives who are not the child's parent.
resources.how: Call the Eldercare Locator or search by ZIP code, and ask your local Area Agency on Aging about help for grandparents and relatives raising children.

resources.name: Generations United: help for grandfamilies
resources.org: Generations United, National Center on Grandfamilies
resources.what: A national organization working for grandparents and other relatives raising children. It explains programs and laws in plain words, including state laws on enrolling a child in school and consenting to health care.
resources.how: Start with Grandfamilies.org, its library of state laws and topics, or the guide to the caregiver support program for relatives raising children.

resources.name: National Maternal Mental Health Hotline
resources.what: Free, private support for anyone who is pregnant or has had a baby and feels sad, anxious or overwhelmed. Counselors answer any hour, in English and Spanish.
resources.how: Call or text. You do not have to be in a crisis to reach out.

resources.name: Postpartum Support International
resources.what: PSI has Support Coordinators in every US state who can talk with you about postpartum depression, anxiety and other struggles around pregnancy and birth, and point you to local help.
resources.how: Call the HelpLine or open the PSI site and choose United States to find help in your area. This is not an emergency line. If you are in crisis, call or text 988.

resources.name: National Parent & Youth Helpline
resources.what: Free, confidential emotional support for parents and caregivers when parenting feels like too much. Trained specialists answer by call, text or live chat any hour.
resources.how: Call, text or chat. You do not have to be in a crisis.

resources.name: SAMHSA National Helpline: mental health and substance use
resources.org: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration
resources.what: Free, private referrals to treatment and support for mental health or substance use, any hour, every day of the year.
resources.how: Call and describe what you need. They can refer you to local services.

resources.name: MomCo (formerly MOPS): moms groups
resources.what: A nonprofit that gathers moms in small groups, in person and online. It began as Mothers of Preschoolers and has Christian roots, so ask a group how it runs before you go.
resources.how: Use Find a Group to see meetups near you or online. Ask whether membership or a fee is needed.

resources.name: MOMS Club: local chapters for at-home moms
resources.what: A nonprofit with local chapters for at-home mothers. Chapters plan playgroups, outings, moms' nights out and service projects.
resources.how: Open the chapter list and find the chapter for your area. Local chapters set their own dues, so ask before you join.

resources.name: Military OneSource special needs consultations
resources.what: Free consultants help military families with special education, TRICARE, EFMP and local services. Retirees and honorably discharged members can use it for one year after leaving service.
resources.how: Call any time or start a chat to set up a phone or video meeting.

resources.name: Exceptional Family Member Program (EFMP)
resources.what: Active duty families sign up a family member with special medical or school needs. This helps the military plan moves and support around those needs. Some TRICARE programs require it.
resources.how: Contact the EFMP office at your base, or call Military OneSource.

resources.name: CHAMPVA health coverage for veterans' children
resources.what: Health coverage for children of veterans rated permanently and totally disabled by a service-connected condition (or who died from one), if the family cannot get TRICARE. It usually ends at 18, or 23 for full-time students. A child who could not support themselves before 18 may stay covered.
resources.how: Check if you qualify and apply on VA.gov, or ask your county veterans service officer to help.

resources.name: National Call Center for Homeless Veterans
resources.what: Free, confidential help any hour for veterans who are homeless or about to lose their housing. Family members can call for a veteran.
resources.how: Call or chat online. A trained VA counselor connects you with housing help near you.

resources.name: Veterans Crisis Line
resources.what: Free, confidential support any hour for veterans, service members and their families and friends. You do not have to be enrolled in VA health care.
resources.how: Dial 988 and press 1, text 838255, or chat on the website.

resources.name: CDC milestone checklists and Milestone Tracker app
resources.org: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
resources.what: Free checklists show what most children do at each age, from 2 months to 5 years. They come in English and Spanish, and there is a free phone app.
resources.how: Fill out the checklist for your child's age. Take it to your child's next doctor visit. You do not need a diagnosis to ask for help.

resources.name: Find your state's early intervention program
resources.org: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
resources.what: Every state has free early intervention for children under 3 who are behind or have a disability. You can call yourself. You do not need a doctor's note.
resources.how: Look up your state's number and ask for a free evaluation. If your child is 3 or older, call your public school district instead.

resources.name: Your state's Parent Training and Information Center
resources.org: Center for Parent Information and Resources
resources.what: Every state has a free parent center for families of children with any disability, from birth to age 26. Staff help with school plans, meetings and your rights.
resources.how: Find your state on the map. Call before your next school meeting.

resources.name: Family-to-Family Health Information Center
resources.what: Parents who have been there help other families with doctors, insurance, Medicaid and disability services. There is one in every state.
resources.how: Find your state's center on the map and call or email them.

resources.name: Parent to Parent: get matched with another parent
resources.what: A trained volunteer parent whose child has a similar disability calls you, listens and shares what helped them. It is free.
resources.how: Find your state's Parent to Parent program on the map and ask to be matched.

resources.name: Autism Society National Helpline
resources.what: Trained staff help families find autism services, support groups and local chapters. This is not a crisis line.
resources.how: Call on a weekday or fill out the online form. Ask about the chapter in your state.

resources.name: National Resource Center on ADHD helpline
resources.what: A helpline answers questions about ADHD: diagnosis, treatment, school help and local support groups. Spanish speakers are available.
resources.how: Call the ADHD helpline, or use the parent toolkits on the website.

resources.name: National Respite Locator
resources.what: Respite gives family caregivers a short break while someone trained cares for your child. This search finds respite programs and ways to pay for them.
resources.how: Search by state. The list is not complete, so also ask your county or state disability office.

resources.name: SSI for children with disabilities
resources.what: Monthly payments for children with serious disabilities in families with low income and savings. In most states, SSI also means Medicaid. At 18, Social Security checks again using adult rules.
resources.how: Start online or call for an appointment. Have medical and school records ready.

resources.name: NAMI Basics and the NAMI HelpLine
resources.what: NAMI Basics is a free 6-week class for parents and caregivers of children and teens with mental health symptoms, taught by parents who have been there. It is offered in person or online. The HelpLine gives information and support. It is not a crisis line.
resources.how: Find a class through your local NAMI or take the online version. Call the HelpLine on weekdays.

resources.name: Toys for Tots: ask for toys for your kids
resources.org: Marine Toys for Tots, U.S. Marine Corps Reserve
resources.what: Toys for Tots gives new toys to children whose families cannot afford Christmas gifts. Every area runs its own campaign with its own dates: some take requests from families into late November or December, and some give toys only through local charities, schools and social services.
resources.how: Find the campaign for your area and open its Request a Toy page. If requests have closed, use the campaign's Contact page and ask which local groups are giving out its toys.

resources.name: Salvation Army Angel Tree and Christmas help
resources.what: Many local Salvation Army offices give Christmas gifts, and some give a holiday food box, to children in families with low incomes. Angel Tree usually serves children 12 and younger. Each office sets its own sign-up dates, and many close in the fall.
resources.how: Enter your ZIP code at SAAngelTree.org. If your area is not on it, or sign-up has closed, call your nearest Salvation Army and ask whether any Christmas help, a waiting list or a food box is still open.

resources.name: USPS Operation Santa: a letter to Santa
resources.what: Children and families write to Santa, and people across the country adopt the letters and send the gifts asked for. It is open to families in the continental U.S., Hawaii and Puerto Rico. Not every letter is adopted.
resources.how: Include your first and last name, your full return address and the wishes in order. Mail it to Santa Claus, 123 Elf Road, North Pole, 88888 with a First-Class stamp, postmarked by December 5, 2026.

resources.name: Angel Tree for children with a parent in prison
resources.org: Prison Fellowship (a different program from the Salvation Army's Angel Tree)
resources.what: A local church delivers a Christmas gift to the child on behalf of their mom or dad in prison.
resources.how: The parent in prison signs the children up on an application from the prison chaplain, sent out each summer. If you are raising the children, you can ask Prison Fellowship to mail an application to the parent. A church contacts you, usually October to December, if an application was received.

resources.name: Operation Homefront: holiday meals and toys for military families
resources.what: Holiday Meals for Military events give a holiday meal to military families, mainly junior enlisted families (E-1 to E-6), and Holiday Toy Drive events give toys. Events are held in certain cities, most near bases, through December.
resources.how: Open the list of Holiday Meals events and register for one near you. For toy drives, the Holiday Toys page says to follow Operation Homefront on Facebook to hear when sign-up opens in your area.

resources.name: Find someone in federal prison
resources.what: The Bureau of Prisons' locator finds a person in federal prison by name or register number. State prisons and county jails each have their own search: use your state's department of corrections, or call the county sheriff's office.
resources.how: Search by name, or by the federal register number if you have it. Write down the prison name and register number; you will need them for mail, money and visits.

resources.name: Mail, calls, money and visits in federal prison
resources.what: The Bureau of Prisons explains how to send money to someone in federal prison (by MoneyGram, Western Union or the mail), and the rules for mail, phone calls and visits. Visitors must be on the person's approved visiting list.
resources.how: Read the sending-money steps before you pay, and check the prison's own page for visiting days and hours before you travel.

resources.name: Helping young children when a parent is incarcerated
resources.what: Free videos, printables, a read-aloud storybook and tips for talking with children about a parent's incarceration, getting ready for a visit and staying connected. Made for ages up to about 6, in English and Spanish, with a workshop on taking care of yourself as the caregiver.
resources.how: Start with "Coping With Incarceration" and the storybook "In My Family". Watch a video together before a first visit so your child knows what to expect.

resources.name: Can a past cannabis record be cleared? Every state compared
resources.what: A state-by-state table of whether and how a past cannabis record can be sealed, expunged or pardoned, with the source for each state and the date it was checked. For other records, ask legal aid in your state.
resources.how: Find your state in the table and follow its source. Ohio has a full step-by-step walkthrough for marijuana and other records.

resources.name: If your loved one is a veteran
resources.what: VA has justice outreach specialists for veterans in jail and court, and re-entry specialists for veterans in prison. VA pay is cut during a long prison stay after a felony conviction, and a spouse, children or dependent parents can ask VA for part of the money it holds back. VA does not send it unless the family applies.
resources.how: Read the guide's page on veterans in the justice system, then apply for the family's share on VA Form 21-0788.
